overview.what_it_is: A diagnostic review lesson in which learners recall the PTE Academic item types studied in Lessons 1–7, identify their strengths and problem areas, compare responses with a partner or group, convert difficulties into practical improvement strategies, and choose targeted extra practice. It is not a separate scored PTE item type; it is a structured learning process for improving speaking, writing, reading, and listening performance.

format_facts.label: Primary purpose
format_facts.value: Review earlier item types, diagnose difficulties, and create specific improvement actions.

format_facts.label: Interaction format
format_facts.value: Individual reflection followed by pair, small-group, or whole-class discussion.

format_facts.label: Main review cycle
format_facts.value: Recall the task, identify the skill, describe the problem, compare evidence, choose a solution, and repeat the task.

format_facts.label: Item types emphasized
format_facts.value: Answer short question; Read aloud; Repeat sentence; Reading: Fill in the blanks; Reading & writing: Fill in the blanks; Select missing word; Highlight incorrect words; and Summarize written text.

format_facts.label: Items normally deferred
format_facts.value: Reading multiple-choice items and Write essay do not require detailed recap here because they receive further treatment in later lessons.

format_facts.label: Recommended duration
format_facts.value: Approximately 45–60 minutes, with additional time for selected practice tasks.

scoring_factors.name: Accurate task recall
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can correctly explain what each reviewed item type requires and which communicative skills it uses.

scoring_factors.name: Diagnostic specificity
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner identifies a precise difficulty, such as hesitation, weak prediction, poor detail selection, spelling, or loss of concentration, rather than using a vague label such as bad English.

scoring_factors.name: Evidence-based reflection
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether strengths and weaknesses are supported by examples from completed practice responses, recordings, notes, or feedback.

scoring_factors.name: Strategy usefulness
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the proposed solution directly addresses the identified problem and can be practised in a repeatable way.

scoring_factors.name: Transfer across skills
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can connect one underlying skill, such as identifying main ideas or processing language quickly, to several PTE item types.

critical_rules: Do not treat the recap as passive revision; produce written evidence of strengths, weaknesses, causes, and next actions.
Describe one observable problem at a time, such as pausing too long before answering, rather than making a general statement such as speaking is difficult.
Base peer feedback on the response or task requirements, not on personal preference.
Give at least one positive observation before recommending a correction.
Match every solution to the cause of the problem; more practice alone is not a complete strategy.
Repeat a task after feedback whenever possible so that the learner tests whether the new strategy works.
Prioritize high-impact weaknesses or patterns that affect several item types.
Do not spend equal time on every earlier item type when some skills are already secure.

learning_goals: Name the main item types studied in Lessons 1–7 and explain the response required for each one.
Connect each reviewed item type to the speaking, writing, reading, listening, grammar, vocabulary, spelling, pronunciation, or fluency skills it uses.
Identify personal strengths using specific evidence from previous practice.
Identify precise problem areas and distinguish symptoms from likely causes.
Give and receive constructive peer feedback using task-focused language.
Turn each significant problem into a practical strategy and a measurable next step.
Select extra practice according to need rather than repeating every activity.
Complete a short review cycle and record whether performance improves after applying feedback.

core_method.name: REVIEW–DIAGNOSE–SOLVE–REPEAT
core_method.summary: Use a six-stage cycle to recall an item type, examine actual performance, identify the exact problem and its cause, obtain focused feedback, choose one corrective action, and immediately test that action through repeated practice.

steps.detail: Name the item type, describe what appears on screen, state the required response, and identify the main skills involved without first checking the guide.
Examine a previous answer, recording, completed worksheet, practice score, or memory of the task and note what happened.
Write one strength, one precise weakness, and the likely cause of the weakness.
Exchange responses with a familiar partner and ask for one evidence-based positive comment and one high-priority improvement.
Choose one concrete strategy, such as reducing notes to keywords, predicting grammar before listening, or answering immediately with a short phrase.
Attempt a similar task again, apply the selected strategy, and record whether accuracy, fluency, speed, or confidence improved.

core_method.formula: ITEM TYPE + REQUIRED SKILL + OBSERVED PROBLEM + LIKELY CAUSE + ONE STRATEGY + REPEATED TASK = TARGETED IMPROVEMENT

techniques.name: Item-Type Memory Map
techniques.purpose: Rebuild accurate knowledge of earlier PTE tasks and reveal gaps in task understanding.
how_to: Write the names of the item types studied in Lessons 1–7 from memory.
For each item, record the input mode, the required response, and the skills used.
Add one strategy that is essential for successful performance.
Check the completed map against lesson notes only after recalling independently.
Mark uncertain or incorrect entries as priority review areas.
techniques.example: Repeat sentence: input is spoken; response is spoken; main skills are listening, memory, pronunciation, stress, and oral fluency; useful strategy is to retain meaningful chunks rather than isolated words.
techniques.why_it_matters: A learner cannot improve efficiently when the task requirements or scoring-relevant skills are misunderstood.
techniques.common_error: Listing only the item names without explaining what the learner must actually do.

techniques.name: Strength–Problem–Evidence Record
techniques.purpose: Replace vague self-evaluation with specific, observable information.
how_to: Choose one completed practice item.
Write one successful feature of the response.
Write one feature that reduced accuracy, clarity, fluency, or task completion.
Add evidence, such as a missing main point, a long pause, an incorrect word, or an unfinished sentence.
Rate the problem as high, medium, or low priority.
techniques.example: Strength: I understood the topic of the summary passage. Problem: I included too many minor details. Evidence: my sentence mentioned three examples but did not clearly state the writer's main claim.
techniques.why_it_matters: Specific evidence makes it possible to select a strategy that addresses the real weakness.
techniques.common_error: Writing broad comments such as vocabulary is weak without identifying where or how vocabulary caused a problem.

techniques.name: Problem-to-Solution Ladder
techniques.purpose: Develop a corrective strategy that addresses the cause of a problem rather than only its visible symptom.
how_to: State the observed problem in one sentence.
Ask why the problem happened.
Ask whether the cause is task knowledge, language knowledge, processing speed, attention, memory, or test strategy.
Choose one action that directly addresses that cause.
Define how the action will be practised and measured.
techniques.example: Problem: I miss the final word in Select missing word. Cause: I stop following the speaker while considering earlier options. Solution: delay option evaluation, follow the whole argument, and predict the ending from the final sentence and discourse direction.
techniques.why_it_matters: Repeating the same task without changing the underlying process often repeats the same mistake.
techniques.common_error: Using practise more as the only solution without specifying what to practise differently.

techniques.name: Two Stars and One Next Step
techniques.purpose: Make peer assessment balanced, constructive, and easy to apply.
how_to: Listen to or read the complete response before commenting.
Identify two features that supported successful task completion.
Choose only one high-impact improvement for the next attempt.
Link the improvement to a specific part of the response.
Ask the learner to restate the next step in their own words.
techniques.example: Star 1: Your short answer was accurate. Star 2: Your pronunciation was clear. Next step: begin speaking sooner because the pause before the answer was longer than necessary.
techniques.why_it_matters: Limited, prioritized feedback is easier to remember and apply than a long list of corrections.
techniques.common_error: Correcting every minor language issue and leaving the learner unsure which change matters most.

techniques.name: Cross-Skill Pattern Hunt
techniques.purpose: Identify one underlying weakness that affects several PTE item types.
how_to: Review problems from speaking, writing, reading, and listening tasks.
Group similar problems under broader skills such as main-idea recognition, rapid word retrieval, grammar, concentration, or working memory.
Identify which pattern appears most often.
Select a drill that supports several item types.
Track whether improvement transfers to more than one task.
techniques.example: A learner misses the main idea in Summarize written text, Select missing word, and listening review tasks. The shared weakness is following discourse structure, so the learner practises identifying topic sentences, contrast markers, conclusions, and final claims.
techniques.why_it_matters: Improving one shared skill can produce gains across multiple sections of the test.
techniques.common_error: Treating every incorrect response as an unrelated mistake.

techniques.name: Priority Practice Matrix
techniques.purpose: Choose the most useful extra practice when review time is limited.
how_to: List the identified problem areas.
Rate each problem by frequency, impact, and confidence.
Prioritize problems that occur often and affect several item types.
Choose one short drill and one authentic practice item for the highest-priority problem.
Postpone low-impact issues until the major weakness is more stable.
techniques.example: Hesitation affects Answer short question, Read aloud, and Repeat sentence, so immediate-response and chunking drills receive priority over reviewing a single rare vocabulary error.
techniques.why_it_matters: Review time produces better results when it is directed toward high-impact weaknesses.
techniques.common_error: Practising only the easiest or most enjoyable item type.

worked_examples.title: Selecting Details in Summarize Written Text
worked_examples.input: Item type: Summarize written text. Learner reflection: I can identify the topic, but I do not know which details to keep. My summary often contains examples but the main argument is not clear.
worked_examples.decoding: The issue is not basic comprehension of the topic. The learner has difficulty distinguishing the central claim from supporting evidence and therefore gives too much space to examples.
worked_examples.plan: Agree on the main point first, label each remaining detail as essential support or optional example, keep only details that explain or qualify the main point, and compare the revised sentence with a partner.
worked_examples.model_answer: Problem: I include interesting examples before establishing the writer's central message. Likely cause: I treat all factual information as equally important. Strategy: write the main claim in five to ten words, test every detail by asking whether it is necessary to understand that claim, and remove details that only illustrate it. Next practice: revise one earlier summary and then complete one new timed item.

annotations.comment: The weakness is described precisely as poor selection of supporting information.
The learner is confusing examples with essential ideas rather than failing to understand the passage.
The main claim is established before decisions are made about supporting details.
The learner can compare the number and relevance of details before and after revision.

worked_examples.title: Reducing Hesitation in Answer Short Question
worked_examples.input: Learner reflection: I usually understand the question quickly, but I hesitate before speaking because I try to create a complete sentence.
worked_examples.decoding: The task often requires only one word or a short phrase. The learner's desire to produce a full sentence increases response time without improving task completion.
worked_examples.plan: Listen for the key question cue, retrieve the shortest accurate answer, respond immediately, and review accuracy after the attempt rather than editing silently before speaking.
worked_examples.model_answer: Strength: I normally understand what information the question requests. Weakness: I delay my answer while constructing unnecessary grammar. Partner feedback: answer with one word or a short phrase as soon as the answer is known. Practice action: complete ten questions, record the delay before each answer, and aim to respond within approximately one second when confident.

annotations.comment: The learner separates listening comprehension from speaking hesitation.
A short accurate response is prioritized over an unnecessary full sentence.
The recommendation directly addresses the cause of hesitation.
Response delay and answer accuracy can both be monitored.

worked_examples.title: Maintaining Focus in Highlight Incorrect Words
worked_examples.input: Learner reflection: I follow the first part of the recording, but after I click one incorrect word, I lose my place and miss the next difference.
worked_examples.decoding: The main difficulty is attention recovery and eye–ear coordination, not vocabulary knowledge. The physical act of selecting a word interrupts continuous tracking.
worked_examples.plan: Keep the eyes slightly ahead of the audio, use meaning groups rather than individual words, click without rereading previous text, and immediately return attention to the current spoken phrase.
worked_examples.model_answer: Problem: selecting an error interrupts my tracking of the recording. Cause: I look back at the selected word to confirm it. Solution: make one click, do not verify during the recording, and move my eyes to the next phrase immediately. Extra drill: read a transcript while listening and lightly mark substitutions on paper without stopping.

annotations.comment: The learner misses later differences after making an earlier selection.
The interruption comes from checking the previous answer rather than continuing to track the audio.
The strategy protects continuous attention during the one-time recording.
Paper marking develops coordination before returning to computer-based selection.

worked_examples.title: Improving Context Decisions in Fill in the Blanks
worked_examples.input: Learner reflection: I choose a word because its meaning seems suitable, but my answer is often grammatically wrong or does not form a natural phrase.
worked_examples.decoding: The learner is using meaning alone and is not checking part of speech, sentence grammar, collocation, or the wider logical context.
worked_examples.plan: Predict the required grammatical form, identify nearby collocations, compare the meaning of the available choices, insert the best option, and reread the complete sentence.
worked_examples.model_answer: Problem: I select semantically related words without checking how they function in the sentence. Strategy: before looking at the choices, predict whether the blank requires a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, or fixed phrase; then eliminate options that do not fit the grammar or collocation. Final check: reread the sentence and the surrounding sentence to confirm both meaning and flow.

annotations.comment: The learner recognizes that meaning alone is insufficient.
Predicting the part of speech reduces the number of plausible options.
Natural word partnerships are considered alongside grammar.
The final answer must fit the whole passage, not only the words beside the blank.

items.when_to_use: Use when comparing a recent response with an earlier attempt.

items.item: I lost accuracy because...
items.when_to_use: Use when explaining the likely cause of an incorrect response.

items.when_to_use: Use when prioritizing one weakness among several possibilities.

items.item: One change that could improve the next attempt is...
items.when_to_use: Use to give one prioritized and actionable recommendation.

items.when_to_use: Use to connect feedback to a specific moment in the response.

items.when_to_use: Use when suggesting a change to organization, wording, pronunciation, or detail selection.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the recap as a teacher-led lecture.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Learners do not examine their own performance, explain their difficulties, or develop independent problem-solving skills.
common_mistakes.fix: Use individual reflection, pair comparison, group problem-solving, and learner-generated solutions before teacher clarification.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing vague weaknesses such as listening is bad.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A vague diagnosis does not show when the problem occurs or which strategy could correct it.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the exact behaviour, such as losing the next phrase after selecting an answer or missing contrast words near the end of a recording.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Limited study time is spent on secure skills while high-impact weaknesses receive insufficient attention.
common_mistakes.fix: Prioritize problems according to frequency, impact, confidence, and transfer across tasks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving feedback based on preference rather than task requirements.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Comments may encourage changes that do not improve accuracy, fluency, relevance, or comprehension.
common_mistakes.fix: Refer to the required response, the learner's evidence, and the skill being reviewed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving too many corrections at once.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner cannot remember or apply a long list during the next timed attempt.
common_mistakes.fix: Select one high-priority change and test it immediately.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing a strategy that does not match the cause.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: For example, vocabulary study will not directly solve a concentration problem caused by checking earlier answers.
common_mistakes.fix: Identify whether the cause involves language knowledge, task knowledge, attention, memory, speed, or strategy before choosing the drill.

common_mistakes.mistake: Accepting feedback without repeating the task.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner does not discover whether the proposed solution actually improves performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Complete a second attempt or a closely related practice item and compare the result.

common_mistakes.mistake: Recapping Reading multiple-choice and Write essay in excessive detail at this stage.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: It reduces time available for item types that are the intended focus of this recap and that may not receive immediate later review.
common_mistakes.fix: Record urgent questions about those tasks, but keep the main recap focused on the designated homework and feedback items.

time_budget.focus: List reviewed item types, required responses, and associated skills from memory.
Record strengths, precise weaknesses, evidence, and likely causes.
Exchange responses and provide two positive observations plus one next step.
Share common difficulties and develop practical solutions.
Apply one selected strategy to a similar task and compare performance.
Record the next drill, success measure, and date for review.

drills.name: Three-Column Item Recall
drills.instructions: Create three columns labelled item type, required response, and main skills. Complete them from memory for at least eight reviewed item types, then correct the map using lesson notes.

drills.name: One-Minute Problem Diagnosis
drills.instructions: Choose one earlier response and write the problem, evidence, likely cause, and one solution in sixty seconds. Repeat with three different item types.

drills.name: Peer Feedback Exchange
drills.instructions: Give a partner two evidence-based strengths and one prioritized next step. The partner must explain how the suggestion will be applied in the next attempt.

drills.name: Immediate Response Sprint
drills.instructions: Complete ten Answer short question prompts using only the shortest accurate answer. Track hesitation and review errors after the full set.

drills.name: Main-Idea and Support Sort
drills.instructions: Take a short reading passage and classify each note as topic, main claim, essential support, example, or minor detail. Use the result to produce a concise summary plan.

drills.name: Listen–Track–Recover
drills.instructions: Follow a transcript while listening once. Mark a deliberate mismatch without stopping, then move immediately to the next phrase to practise recovery for Highlight incorrect words.

drills.name: Grammar–Meaning–Collocation Check
drills.instructions: For each blank, predict the part of speech, identify possible collocations, compare meanings, insert an answer, and reread the surrounding context.

drills.name: Strategy Retest
drills.instructions: Repeat a similar practice item immediately after feedback and write one sentence explaining whether the chosen strategy improved accuracy, speed, fluency, or confidence.

practice_plan.routine: Use a compact weekly review cycle: select one speaking, one reading or writing, and one listening response; complete the Strength–Problem–Evidence record; receive or simulate focused feedback; apply one correction; repeat a similar item; and record the result in an error-and-strategy log. Revisit recurring problems until the same weakness no longer appears across two or three practice sessions.

mastery_checklist: I can name the reviewed item types without relying immediately on the guide.
I can explain what input I receive and what response I must produce for each item type.
I can connect each task to its main communicative and enabling skills.
I can state at least one specific strength and support it with evidence.
I can describe a problem precisely instead of using a vague label.
I can distinguish the visible error from its likely underlying cause.
I can give a partner balanced, task-focused, and actionable feedback.
I can convert a weakness into one concrete strategy and one practice activity.
I can prioritize review according to impact rather than personal preference.
I can repeat a task after feedback and compare the two attempts.
I can identify one weakness that affects several item types.
I can create a short follow-up study plan with a measurable success criterion.
strategy_notes: The recap lesson is most effective when learners do the explaining, comparing, and problem-solving rather than waiting for complete teacher solutions.
A useful problem statement identifies the task, the exact moment of difficulty, the effect on performance, and the likely cause.
Speaking review should consider response timing, fluency, pronunciation, stress, intonation, accuracy, and whether the response length suits the task.
Writing review should distinguish idea selection, organization, grammar, vocabulary, spelling, punctuation, and compliance with task requirements.
Reading review should examine main-idea recognition, contextual vocabulary, grammar, collocation, logical relationships, and time management.
Listening review should examine attention, prediction, note-taking, sound discrimination, tracking, memory, and understanding of discourse direction.
The best extra practice is not always a complete test item; a short drill may isolate the underlying skill more efficiently.
After isolated practice, return to an authentic or timed item to confirm that the skill transfers to test conditions.
Keep an error-and-strategy log containing the item type, problem, cause, strategy, repeated result, and next review date.
Reading multiple-choice items and Write essay can be briefly noted if urgent difficulties arise, but detailed treatment may be deferred because they are revisited later.

metadata.provenance_note: Enriched from the supplied Chapter 8 recap material and its stated review process for Lessons 1–7. The lesson preserves the source emphasis on learner discussion, self and peer assessment, shared problem-solving, targeted extra practice, and selective recap of designated item types while expanding these ideas into a structured teaching-first diagnostic workflow.
